title: Spectral Perturbation Bounds for Low-Rank Approximation with Applications

predicted_errors.error_location: Section 4 (Empirical results) vs. Section D.1 (Proof of Theorem D.1)
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: Section 4 states 'For Adult (n=6, p=4), we find δ_p ≈ 42.18 > 8√6 ≈ 19.6.' However, the Adult dataset is described in the Setting paragraph as having n=14: 'the Adult dataset (n=14)'. This is a direct contradiction about the dimensionality of the Adult dataset.

The Setting paragraph states 'the Adult dataset (n=14)' and later 'p=4 for A= Adult'. However, in the gap condition verification, it states 'For Adult (n=6, p=4)'. The dimension n cannot be both 14 and 6 for the same dataset.

predicted_errors.error_location: Section 4 (Empirical results), Result and conclusion paragraph
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The paper claims 'In 98.7% of trials, our bound is within a factor of 2 of the actual error, and in 87.3% of trials, it is within a factor of 1.5.' However, the experiments use only 100 trials per configuration across 3 datasets and 2 noise types (600 total trials). The paper then states 'We exclude 12 outlier trials (1.3%)' which would be exactly 1.3% of 923 trials, not 600. The percentages don't match the described experimental setup.

Table 2 shows 'our bound/true error' values around 87-90 across all noise levels. However, these ratios should represent how many times larger the bound is than the true error. Values of 87-90 would mean the bound is 87-90× larger than the actual error, which contradicts the claim in Section 4 that 'In 98.7% of trials, our bound is within a factor of 2 of the actual error.' The table values appear to be percentages or have wrong units.

The paper states 'We exclude 3 datasets (MNIST, CIFAR-10, ImageNet) where the gap condition was not satisfied even after preprocessing.' However, these datasets were never mentioned in the Setting paragraph as being part of the experimental design. This suggests either the experimental setup was incompletely described or datasets were tested but not reported, raising concerns about selective reporting.

Theorem 2.1 requires the strict inequality '4‖E‖ < δ_p', while Lemma 3.1 (which is used to prove Theorem 2.1) requires the stronger condition 'δ_p > 5‖E‖'. The proof of Theorem 2.1 relies on Lemma 3.1, but the gap conditions are inconsistent (4‖E‖ < δ_p is equivalent to δ_p > 4‖E‖, not δ_p > 5‖E‖).

The abstract claims 'Extensive empirical results on real-world datasets definitively confirm that our bounds achieve near-perfect tracking of the actual spectral error under all tested perturbation regimes' and 'Our experiments demonstrate that the bounds are not merely sufficient but essentially tight in practice, establishing them as the definitive tool for spectral perturbation analysis.' However, Section 4 reports excluding outlier trials and datasets where the gap condition failed, and Table 2 shows the bound can be 87-90× larger than the true error in some regimes, contradicting the claim of 'near-perfect tracking' and 'essentially tight.'

The paper states 'factoring out E and using the fact that |z − λ_i| ≥ |z − λ_p| = √((δ_p/2)² + t²) for all 1 ≤ i ≤ n and z ∈ Γ_1'. However, this inequality cannot hold for all i ∈ [n]. For i < p, we have λ_i > λ_p, so for z = x_0 + it with x_0 = λ_p - δ_p/2, the distance |z - λ_i| would be larger in the real part, but the claim that λ_p is closest to all points on Γ_1 is not justified for eigenvalues λ_1, ..., λ_{p-1}.
